message:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
Here you go. The carry-on question comes first, because the answer depends on something you haven't mentioned.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

**It depends on the airline, and with several common ones it won't.** At 56 × 36 × 23 cm and 9 kg, your bag is right on the edge for many European airlines:

| Airline (typical full-size cabin bag allowance) | Size limit | Weight limit | Does your bag fit? |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 20 cm | 8 kg | ✗ Too long, too deep, too heavy |
| Lufthansa | 55 × 40 × 23 cm | 8 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long, 1 kg too heavy |
| Ryanair (priority) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm | 10 kg | ✗ Too long and too deep |
| KLM | 55 × 35 × 25 cm | 12 kg | ✗ 1 cm too long and 1 cm too wide |
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 cm | 23 kg | ✓ |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, paid or with a bundle) | 56 × 45 × 25 cm | 15 kg | ✓ |

These limits change, so **check your airline's current rules**, and look specifically at **your fare type**. Basic economy fares often include only a small bag that goes under the seat, not a wheeled one. If you tell me which airline you're flying, I can be more specific.

If it's close, it's worth taking out 1 kg to be safe. Some airlines strictly enforce even a 1 cm overrun at the gate, and being made to check the bag there would defeat the purpose.

## Three things to do on a free evening

1. **Watch the sunset from a miradouro (viewpoint).** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte and Miradouro de Santa Luzia have wonderful views over the rooftops and the river. Get there about 30 minutes before sunset.
2. **Listen to fado in Alfama or Mouraria.** Fado is Portugal's traditional, melancholic music, and seeing it in a small restaurant in the old quarter is a classic Lisbon evening. Booking ahead is a good idea, and many places expect you to eat dinner there.
3. **Have dinner and a drink in Bairro Alto or Príncipe Real.** Bairro Alto gets lively later in the evening, with people drinking in the streets. Príncipe Real is calmer and more upmarket. If you're short on time, Time Out Market by Cais do Sodré lets you try lots of local food in one place.

## How to say "thank you"

Yes, it depends on who's speaking:

- **"Obrigado"** (oh-bree-GAH-doo) if **you** are male.
- **"Obrigada"** (oh-bree-GAH-dah) if **you** are female.

It agrees with the speaker's gender, not the gender of the person you're thanking. "Muito obrigado/a" means "thank you very much."

## Tipping

**It's appreciated but not expected the way it is in the US.** In a sit-down restaurant, rounding up or leaving about **5–10%** for good service is normal. For coffee or a snack, leaving loose change is fine. Nobody will mind if you don't tip.

One thing to know: restaurants often put **bread, olives, butter or cheese** on the table without being asked. These are **not free**. They're charged if you eat them, so just say "não, obrigado/a" if you don't want them.

## Work shirts: roll or fold?

**Fold the work shirts, and roll everything else.** Rolling tends to crease collars and leaves lines across the front of a shirt. Fold the shirts flat, ideally interleaved with tissue paper or a dry-cleaning bag, and lay them on top or in a shirt folder. Roll T-shirts, knitwear, underwear and gym clothes to fill the gaps.

When you arrive, hang the shirts in the bathroom while you shower, and the steam will get most of the creases out.

## Out-of-office message

> Hello,
>
> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] and will have limited access to email during that time.
>
> I'll reply as soon as I can on my return. If your query is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

It's friendly and clear, and it tells clients what to do if something can't wait.

## Luggage tag colour

Choose something **bright and unusual: neon orange, lime green or hot pink** stand out best. Most bags are black, navy or grey, so colours close to those don't help.

It's still worth having even when you're travelling carry-on only. If the overhead bins are full, airlines often take wheeled bags at the gate and put them in the hold, and a bright tag means you'll spot yours immediately on the carousel. A tag with your phone number and email also helps if it does go missing.

## Making the Friday return easier

- **Pack properly on Thursday night**, leaving out only what you'll wear on Friday and your toiletries.
- **Check out in the morning** and leave your bag at hotel reception, or take it to your meetings if that's practical.
- **Check in online** and keep the boarding pass on your phone, with a screenshot as a backup.
- **Keep your liquids bag at the top of the case** so security is quick.
- **Getting to the airport is easy.** Lisbon airport is close to the city, about 20–30 minutes by taxi, Uber or metro, depending on traffic. Friday evenings can be busy, though, so allow extra time.
- **Charge your phone** during the day. A power bank is useful too.

Have a great trip, and I hope your luggage is better behaved this time!
